pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written tfn.t; the name’s root is tf, “to spit” or “to be moist”.
Conventionally vocalised “Tefnut”; the feminine ending marks her as the moisture-principle.

pronunciation.note: Her name belongs to the tf-family: in one cosmogony she and Shu are spat into being by the creator — the moisture and air of the first breath.

domains.title: Goddess of Moisture, the Dew and the Rain
domains.subtitle: The Spat-Forth One, Sister of the Air
domains.lead: Tfnt — Tefnut — is water in its gentlest forms: the humidity of the first morning of the world, the dew, the rare and precious rain. With her twin Shu, the air, she is the first pair the creator produced — and in the myth that names her, the creator spat them both into existence.

cards.name: The First Moisture
cards.desc: The humidity that preceded creation’s drying-out; twin and consort of Shu the air.

cards.name: The Solar Eye
cards.desc: As the Eye of Ra she fled to Nubia in lioness form and had to be fetched back by Thoth or Shu.

cards.name: Lioness of the Waters
cards.desc: Shown as a lioness or lioness-headed woman — the same dangerous femininity as Sekhmet and Bastet.

cards.name: Mistress of the Dew
cards.desc: Her moisture is the world’s lubricant — the dew on which the sun’s first dawn condensed.

mythology.lead: Tefnut’s mythology is concentrated at the world’s beginning and in the great Eye-of-Ra cycle. As one of the first two beings she needs few adventures — but the one she has, the flight to Nubia and the embassy that retrieves her, became one of the most told and most illustrated stories of the New Kingdom.

myths.title: The Spat-Forth Pair
myths.text: In the Memphite and Heliopolitan accounts the creator — Atum or Ra — produced his first two children by spitting (tf) and sneezing: Tefnut the moisture and Shu the air. Their names are the verbs of that first physiology; the world’s atmosphere is the afterbirth of the god’s own body.

myths.title: The Flight to Nubia
myths.text: When the creator grew old, men plotted against him — and his Eye, sent to punish them, abandoned her post in fury and fled south as a raging lioness. Egypt withered without her. Shu or Thoth was sent to coax her home with the Destruction of Mankind tale’s rhetoric of flattery; her return, pacified, restores the inundation and the sun’s order.

myths.title: The Return of the Goddess
myths.text: The literary composition ‘The Return of the Eye’ gives Tefnut’s wanderings their fullest poetic form — the goddess who leaves, rages, is sung back, and returns transformed from destroyer to blessing. It is the mythic template behind every Egyptian pacification ritual of dangerous goddesses.

myths.title: Mother of Nut and Geb
myths.text: With Shu she bore Nut the sky and Geb the earth — the second divine generation. As grandmother of Osiris, Isis, Seth and Nephthys she stands at the head of every royal pedigree; the titulary of kings names her among the oldest company of the gods.

lore.syncretism: Tefnut merges almost completely with her sister-forms of the solar Eye — Sekhmet, Bastet, Hathor, Mut — each a local face of the one dangerous goddess. Greeks knew her chiefly through Plutarch as one of the primal elements, moisture to Shu’s air; modern study treats her and Shu as the key to Egypt’s ‘physical’ cosmogony, where the first creatures are states of the atmosphere.
lore.culturalLegacy: The spit-and-sneeze cosmogony remains a favourite exhibit of Egyptian theology’s concreteness — the first act of creation as a bodily reflex. Her lioness form fed the iconography of Egyptian goddesses generally; and the Leiden ‘Return of the Eye’ is a set text of Middle Egyptian literature courses for its perfect rhetoric.
lore.extendedMeditation: Tfnt: four consonants, one syllable of certainty. She is the moisture on the name itself — the breath between the consonants that every reader must supply. Restoring her in plain letters keeps the dew exactly where the Egyptians left it: everywhere, and unmarked.

sources.name: Book of the Heavenly Cow (Destruction of Mankind)
Leiden Papyrus I 384 (Return of the Eye)

lore.archaeology: She appears with Shu flanking the solar barque in tomb and temple programmes from the Old Kingdom onward — the twin supports of the sun’s journey. Fine lioness-headed examples survive in the Ramesside temples of the Theban west bank and in the Louvre’s statuary of the solar triads.
lore.cult: Her cult was fused with the Eye-of-Ra complexes: at Leontopolis and in the Mut precincts she received pacification rites, her dangerous return celebrated as the restoration of order. As primal moisture she needed little separate cult — she was already in every breath and every dawn.
lore.iconography: A woman with the head of a lioness, crowned with the sun disc and uraeus when in her Eye aspect, or simply standing beside Shu as half of the first pair. Her skin may be blue-green like watered things; the cobra and lioness share her fiercer representations.
lore.reception: Through Plutarch and the Hermetic element-theories she entered late-antique natural philosophy as the Egyptian ‘moisture principle’. Modern comparative religion uses the Shu–Tefnut pair as the textbook case of a cosmogony built from meteorological personifications.
